html:
Istanbul is the largest city of Turkey, on both banks of the Bosporus, the strait between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. It sits on two continents, Europe and Asia. Before 1453 it was Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire; see Constantinople for that story.

Mehmed II took the city in the siege of 1453 and made it the capital of the Ottoman Empire. He repopulated it with Muslims, Christians and Jews from across his lands and turned Hagia Sophia into a mosque. Under Süleyman and his architect Sinan, new mosques rose on its hills, and the Grand Bazaar was the heart of a trade that ran from Persia to Venice. The Galata Tower watched over the merchant quarter across the Golden Horn.

In the 1700s and 1800s the city led the empire's reforms: the first Ottoman Muslim printing press in 1727, and later banks, railways and newspapers. As the empire fell into debt, the Ottoman Public Debt Administration ran part of its revenue from here.

After the First World War the new Republic of Turkey moved its capital to Ankara in 1923, and the city's name became officially Istanbul in 1930. It grew from about one million people in 1950 to over fifteen million, with migrants from all of Anatolia. It remains Turkey's centre of business, from the stock exchange to the Marmaray rail tunnel under the Bosporus, and the home of writers such as Orhan Pamuk.
